commanders: Özdemiroğlu Osman Pasha & Kılıç Ali Pasha vs. Mehmed II Giray & Safa Giray
importance: The Ottoman Navy and land forces broke the 40-day siege of Caffa, deposed the rebellious Mehmed II Giray, and installed Islam II Giray II as the Ottoman-appointed Khan of Crimea.
casualties: Heavy rebel losses; Mehmed II Giray pursued and executed

name: Second Expedition & Battle in the Andal Desert
commanders: Gazi Ferhad Pasha & Islam II Giray II vs. Saadet Giray & Nogay/Cossack Allies
importance: Following a counter-revolt by Mehmed's sons backed by Nogays and Russian ties, Ferhad Pasha and Ottoman reinforcements decisively defeated the rebels in the Andal Desert near Caffa, firmly securing direct Ottoman suzerainty over the Crimean Khanate.

name: Safavid Recapture of Tabriz
commanders: Shah Abbas I vs Ottomans
importance: Shah Abbas I retook Tabriz.

name: Safavid Siege of Yerevan (1603)
commanders: Shah Abbas I vs Ottomans
importance: Yerevan captured by Safavids.

name: Battle of Urmia
commanders: Safavids vs Ottomans
importance: Major Safavid victory.

name: Battle of Sufiyan
commanders: Safavids vs Ottomans
importance: Decisive Safavid victory over Ottoman field army.

name: Siege of Yerevan (1616)
commanders: Ottomans vs Safavids
importance: Ottoman siege failed.

name: Battle of Sufiyan (1618)
commanders: Safavids vs Ottomans
importance: Safavid victory.

name: Capture of Baghdad (1623)
commanders: Shah Abbas I vs Ottomans
importance: Shah Abbas I retook Baghdad.

name: First Ottoman Siege of Baghdad (1625–1626)
commanders: Ottomans vs Safavids
importance: Ottoman failure.

name: Capture of Yerevan (1635)
commanders: Murad IV vs Safavids
importance: Ottoman victory, though temporary.

name: Capture of Tabriz (1635)

importance: Brief Ottoman occupation.

commanders: Murad IV vs Safavids
importance: Baghdad permanently recovered.

commanders: Crimean-Ottoman vs Russia
importance: Checked northern expansion.

name: Tokhtamysh's sack of Moscow
commanders: Tokhtamysh (Golden Horde) vs. Muscovite defenders
importance: Retaliation following Kulikovo; Tokhtamysh captured and burned Moscow, restoring Tatar suzerainty over the Russian principalities.

name: Edigu's siege of Moscow
commanders: Edigu (Nogai/Golden Horde) vs. Vasily I of Moscow
importance: The powerful emir Edigu besieged Moscow, devastating surrounding lands until Prince Vasily I agreed to pay a heavy ransom.

name: Tatar raid on Moscow (Mazovsha)
commanders: Mazovsha (Tatar prince) vs. Muscovite garrison
importance: A sudden raid by Nogai-Tatar forces that burned the posads (suburbs) of Moscow before being repelled.

name: Akhmat Khan's campaign
commanders: Akhmat Khan (Great Horde) vs. Ivan III
importance: Akhmat Khan sacked Aleksin as a prelude to asserting Great Horde dominance, testing Muscovite readiness prior to the 1480 Ugra standoff.

name: First Muscovite-Crimean War
commanders: Crimean Khanate vs. Tsardom of Russia
importance: Marked the breakdown of the alliance between Moscow and Crimea following the collapse of the Great Horde, initiating centuries of border warfare.

name: Crimean raids into Muscovite borderlands
commanders: Crimean Tatars vs. Muscovite border garrisons
importance: Continuous deep-penetration raids targeting Ryazan and southern Muscovite border territories.

name: Crimean raid on Tula
commanders: Crimean Tatars vs. Muscovite forces
importance: Major Tatar raiding expedition intercepted and defeated near Tula by Muscovite frontier forces.

name: Sahib Giray's campaign
commanders: Sahib Giray vs. Ivan the Terrible's forces
importance: Crimean-Ottoman backed campaign repelled decisively at the Oka River defense line.

name: Devlet I Giray's siege of Tula
commanders: Devlet I Giray vs. Muscovite garrison
importance: Occurred concurrently with Ivan the Terrible's Kazan campaign; Devlet Giray attempted to divert Russian forces by besieging Tula but was beaten back.

name: Battle of Marciano (Scannagallo)
commanders: Gian Giacomo Medici vs. Piero Strozzi
importance: Destroyed the main Franco-Sienese field army and ensured the eventual fall of Siena.

name: Battle of Renty
commanders: Henry II of France, Francis Duke of Guise vs. Charles V, Emmanuel Philibert
importance: Secured French control of the Three Bishoprics despite failing to produce a decisive strategic breakthrough.

name: Siege of Siena
commanders: Gian Giacomo Medici vs. Blaise de Monluc
importance: Ended the independence of the Republic of Siena and paved the way for its annexation by Florence.
casualties: Heavy military and civilian losses during the prolonged siege.

name: Battle of Sudbishchi
commanders: Ivan Sheremetev vs. Devlet I Giray
result: Indecisive tactical engagement / Russian defensive stand
importance: A fierce battle where a small Russian detachment bravely held off a vastly superior Crimean Tatar army, inflicting heavy casualties.

name: Gazi II Giray's raid on Moscow
commanders: Gazi II Giray vs. Boris Godunov's forces
importance: The last major Crimean raid to reach the walls of Moscow; repelled by Russian artillery and mobile field forces.

name: Crimean raids during the Smolensk War
commanders: Crimean Tatars vs. Tsardom of Russia
importance: Tatars exploited Russia's preoccupation with Poland during the Smolensk War to devastate southern border districts.
casualties: Massive civilian abductions and property loss.

name: Meñli I Giray's sack of Kiev
commanders: Meñli I Giray vs. Lithuanian garrison
importance: Meñli I Giray captured and burned Kiev, sending rich spoils (including a golden chalice and paten from the cathedral) to Ivan III.

name: Tatar raids during Poland's Moldavian campaign
commanders: Crimean Tatars vs. Polish-Lithuanian forces
importance: Interference by Crimean forces that contributed to the Polish disaster at the Cosmin Forest.

name: Battle of Kletsk
commanders: Michael Glinski vs. Crimean Tatars
importance: A decisive defeat of a major Crimean raiding party deep inside Belarusian territories by Hetman Michael Glinski.
casualties: Thousands of Tatars killed or liberated captives freed.

name: Battle of Lopushno / Vishnevets
commanders: Constantine Ostrogski vs. Crimean Tatars
importance: Brilliant tactical victory by Constantine Ostrogski, routing a major Tatar raiding force.

name: Clash near Novgorod-Seversky
commanders: Lithuanian-Polish border forces vs. Crimean Tatars
importance: Highlight of ongoing frontier instability along the Lithuanian-Muscovite-Tatar borderlands.

name: Battle of Olszanica
commanders: Ochakiv Tatars vs. Lithuanian force
importance: Ochakiv and Crimean forces overwhelmed local Lithuanian defenses in Ruthenia.

name: Battle of Kaniv
commanders: Constantine Ostrogski vs. Crimean Tatars
importance: Major routing of a Tatar raiding army returning with plunder from Volhynia.
casualties: Heavy Tatar casualties; thousands of captives freed.

name: Crimean raid into Polish Ruthenia
commanders: Crimean Tatars vs. Polish Crown forces
importance: Deep incursion into Polish border provinces during periods of fragile diplomacy.
casualties: Heavy local property and captive losses.

name: Cossack-Tatar border clashes
commanders: Zaporozhian Cossacks vs. Crimean Khanate
importance: Escalating retaliatory raids across the Wild Fields between Cossack hosts and Crimean forces.

name: Battle of Zboriv
commanders: Bohdan Khmelnytsky & Islam III Giray vs. John II Casimir (Poland)
result: Cossack-Tatar tactical advantage / Treaty of Zboriv
importance: Combined Cossack-Tatar forces cornered the Polish royal army, resulting in the favorable Treaty of Zboriv granting autonomy to Cossack Ukraine.

name: Battle of Berestechko
commanders: John II Casimir vs. Bohdan Khmelnytsky & Islam III Giray
importance: The Crimean Khan abandoned the Cossacks mid-battle and took Khmelnytsky hostage, leading to a catastrophic collapse of the rebel alliance.

name: Fall of Bakhchysarai
commanders: Ivan Sirko vs. Selim I Giray
importance: Cossack forces bypassed Perekop, sacked and destroyed the Crimean capital of Bakhchysarai, and forced Khan Selim I Giray to flee
casualties: Heavy destruction of Bakhchysarai; widespread raiding and capture of prisoners

name: Battle of Batih
commanders: Bohdan Khmelnytsky & Crimean allies vs. Marcin Kalinowski (Poland)
importance: Total destruction of a Polish field army, serving as a brutal revenge for Berestechko and execution of Polish prisoners by Tatar allies.
casualties: Virtually the entire Polish army annihilated.

name: Capture of the Peñón of Algiers
commanders: Hayreddin Barbarossa vs. Don Martin de Vargas (Spanish Garrison)
importance: Renewed Ottoman support enabled Hayreddin Barbarossa to capture the Spanish fortress of El Peñón de Argel after a 22-day artillery siege, establishing Algiers as a primary base for Barbary corsair operations and securing Ottoman rule for three centuries
casualties: Heavy Spanish garrison losses (only 25 survivors captured); commander Don Martin de Vargas cudgelled to death

name: Battle of Sokhoista
commanders: King Bagrat III of Imereti & King Luarsab I of Kartli vs. Ottoman Empire forces
importance: Fought on the Sokhoista field near Pasinler; the last major united stand of Georgian dynasts against Ottoman expansion ended in a heavy defeat due to internal dissent, establishing Ottoman hegemony over Samtskhe and securing southwestern Caucasus control

name: First Siege of Jeddah
commanders: Lopo Soares de Albergaria vs. Selman Reis & Amir Husain al-Kurdi
importance: A naval and land engagement in the harbor of Jeddah where a Portuguese expeditionary force under Lopo Soares de Albergaria failed to capture the heavily fortified port defended by Selman Reis and Egyptian Mamluk forces, forcing a Portuguese withdrawal and subsequent blockade
casualties: Several Portuguese ships damaged or burned; Portuguese resupply capture resulting in 16 sailors imprisoned and sent to Constantinople

name: Battle of Formentera
commanders: Aydin Reis vs. Rodrigo Portuondo
importance: Fought off the island of Formentera; an Ottoman fleet under Aydin Reis ambushed and overwhelmed a Spanish galley squadron led by Rodrigo Portuondo, capturing seven of the eight Spanish galleys after Portuondo's flagship was isolated and taken
casualties: Heavy Spanish losses, including the death of commander Rodrigo Portuondo and capture of most of the fleet's galleys; 1,000 Muslim galley slaves liberated

name: Battle of Alborán
commanders: Bernardino de Mendoza vs. Ali Hamet & General Caramani
importance: Fought off the Isle of Alborán following an Ottoman pirate raid on Gibraltar; a Spanish fleet under Bernardino de Mendoza intercepted and crushed Ali Hamet's Barbary fleet, capturing 10 ships, sinking another, and freeing hundreds of Christian slaves
casualties: Heavy Ottoman losses (over 700 killed, 427 captured); Spanish forces suffered 137 dead and ~500 wounded, including commander Mendoza

name: Venetian Attack on Lepanto (December 1499)
commanders: Republic of Venice vs. Ottoman Empire
importance: Venice attacked Lepanto hoping to regain territory lost in the Battle of Zonchio the previous year; Kemal Reis sailed from Cefalonia and retook the city from the Venetians, after which he based his fleet there for repairs (April–May 1500) using 15,000 Ottoman craftsmen brought in from the surrounding area

name: Ottoman Bombardment of Corfu
commanders: Kemal Reis (Ottoman Empire) vs. Venetian ports on Corfu
importance: Kemal Reis's fleet bombarded Venetian ports on Corfu en route to the main objective of the campaign, the siege of Modon

name: Siege of Modon and Battle of Modon (Second Battle of Lepanto)
commanders: Kemal Reis (Ottoman Empire, 220 ships) vs. Melchiorre Trevisan & Girolamo Contarini (Republic of Venice, 66 ships)
importance: Kemal Reis besieged Modon from the sea; the Venetian relief fleet, first led by Trevisan (who died of illness en route on 17 July) and then Contarini, was engaged over two days of naval combat. On the first day (20 July) only an artillery exchange occurred before Contarini withdrew; on the second attempt the Venetian wings initially flanked the Ottoman fleet and inflicted damage, but Ottoman numerical superiority allowed their galleys to encircle the Venetians, sinking a galley that tried to recall four fleeing ships, until Contarini ordered a full retreat to Zante at nightfall. Modon capitulated on 9 August, with most defenders killed fighting and women and children enslaved. Contarini was subsequently criticized by fellow captains for engaging too large an enemy fleet
casualties: One Venetian galley sunk during the battle; four galleys fled the formation; upon Modon's fall, most of the garrison died fighting or were killed, with women and children taken into slavery; only a few men escaped by small boat to Zante to report the news

name: Capture of Coron
commanders: Kemal Reis (Ottoman Empire) vs. Venetian garrison and shipping
importance: Following a violent storm that prevented the Venetian armada from attempting another relief effort, Kemal Reis captured Coron along with a Venetian brigantine, marking the loss of the second of the 'two eyes of the Republic' alongside Modon

name: Sinking of the Venetian Galley Lezza off Sapientza
commanders: Kemal Reis (Ottoman Empire) vs. Venetian galley Lezza
importance: Kemal Reis sailed toward the island of Sapientza after capturing Coron, sinking the Venetian galley Lezza as part of the continued mopping-up phase of the campaign

name: Ottoman Assault on Voiussa
commanders: Kemal Reis (Ottoman Empire) vs. local defenders
importance: Part of Kemal Reis's continued campaign along the Greek and Albanian coasts following the fall of Modon and Coron

name: Ottoman Appearance at Cape Santa Maria (Lefkada)
commanders: Kemal Reis (Ottoman Empire)
result: N/A (show of force, no engagement recorded)
importance: Final stop of Kemal Reis's 1500 campaign before he returned to Constantinople in November; part of a broader pattern of Ottoman cavalry raids that reached as far as Venetian territory in northern Italy during this period

name: Siege of the Castle of Saint George (Cephalonia)
commanders: Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba (Spain, aiding Venice) vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: With Spanish assistance, Venice recovered Cephalonia — the sole significant Venetian reversal of Ottoman gains during this otherwise disastrous campaign; Venice retained this island in the eventual 1502 peace even while recognizing the loss of Modon, Coron, and other territories

name: Ottoman Raid on the Balearic Islands
commanders: Kemal Reis (Ottoman Empire) vs. Spanish coastal defenses
importance: Part of the earliest Ottoman interventions in the western Mediterranean, launched in the context of the Ottoman response to the Fall of Granada and requests for help from Granada's last Muslim ruler against Castile; combined with attacks on Sardinia and Pianosa near Elba. A side effect of the raid was the capture of a Spanish sailor found in possession of an early map of Columbus

name: Truce of Vaucelles
commanders: Charles V; Henry II of France
importance: Suspended hostilities between France and the Habsburgs before fighting resumed later that year.

name: Spanish Invasion of the Papal States
commanders: Fernando Álvarez de Toledo, Duke of Alba vs. Pope Paul IV
importance: Spain occupied much of the Papal States to prevent a Franco-Papal offensive against Naples.

name: Siege of Civitella
commanders: Duke of Alba vs. French forces under François de Guise
importance: Forced the French to abandon their invasion of Naples and secured Spanish control of central Italy.

name: Battle of St. Quentin
commanders: Emmanuel Philibert, Duke of Savoy; Lamoral, Count of Egmont vs. Anne de Montmorency
importance: One of the greatest Habsburg victories of the war, crippling France's field army and shifting the strategic initiative to Spain.
casualties: Heavy French losses; Constable Anne de Montmorency captured.

name: Peace of Cave-Palestrina
commanders: Pope Paul IV; Duke of Alba
importance: The Papal States agreed to neutrality, effectively ending the Papal front of the war.

name: Siege of Calais
commanders: Francis, Duke of Guise vs. Thomas Wentworth
importance: France recaptured Calais, ending over two centuries of continuous English rule in the city.
casualties: English garrison surrendered after moderate losses.

name: Siege of Thionville
commanders: François, Duke of Guise vs. Imperial-Spanish garrison
importance: Strengthened France's hold over the Three Bishoprics and eastern frontier.

name: Raid of the Balearic Islands
commanders: Piyale Pasha; Turgut Reis vs. Spanish defenders
importance: Devastated Spanish possessions in the western Mediterranean and demonstrated continued Ottoman naval supremacy.

name: Battle of Gravelines
commanders: Lamoral, Count of Egmont vs. Paul de Thermes
importance: Destroyed the French invading army in Flanders and compelled Henry II to negotiate peace.
casualties: Heavy French losses; many prisoners captured.

name: Treaties of Cateau-Cambrésis
commanders: Henry II of France; Philip II of Spain; Elizabeth I of England
importance: Ended the Italian War of 1551–1559 and the broader Habsburg–Valois Wars, confirming Spanish predominance in Italy while France retained Calais and the Three Bishoprics.

name: Ottoman Raid on Sardinia (1501)
commanders: Kemal Reis (Ottoman Empire) vs. Spanish/local coastal defenses
importance: Conducted in combination with the Balearic Islands raid as part of the same 1501 western Mediterranean campaign

name: Ottoman Raid on Pianosa (1501)
commanders: Kemal Reis (Ottoman Empire) vs. local coastal defenses
importance: Third target of the combined 1501 western Mediterranean raiding campaign near the island of Elba, alongside the Balearic Islands and Sardinia

name: Ottoman Naval Rescue of Granadan Refugees (1487 and 1492)
commanders: Ottoman Empire (fleet dispatched by Sultan Bayezid II)
importance: In response to appeals from Granada's last Muslim ruler for help against Castile, Bayezid II twice used the Ottoman fleet to rescue Muslim refugees and ferry them to the coast of North Africa — first in 1487, then again when Granada fell in 1492 — establishing the precedent for the later 1501 western Mediterranean raids

name: Treaty Ending the Ottoman–Venetian War (1502)
commanders: Republic of Venice & Ottoman Empire
importance: After suffering repeated setbacks — including the loss of Modon and Coron and Ottoman cavalry raids reaching into northern Italy — Venice sought peace, retaining Cephalonia (recovered with Spanish help) but formally recognizing the rest of the Ottoman territorial gains from the war

name: Battle of Karagak
commanders: King Bagrat III of Imereti & Rostom Gurieli vs. Musa Pasha (Ottoman Empire)
importance: Fought in Meskheti after Ottoman forces under Erzurum beylerbey Musa Pasha besieged Oltisi; King Bagrat III rallied forces to annihilate the remaining Ottoman garrison and decisively defeat the retreating main army, resulting in the death of Musa Pasha
casualties: Heavy Ottoman casualties, including the death of commander Musa Pasha

name: Battle of Khan Yunis
commanders: Hadım Sinan Pasha vs. Janbirdi al-Ghazali
importance: Fought near Gaza and Khan Yunis during the Ottoman-Mamluk War; Ottoman forces under Grand Vizier Hadım Sinan Pasha repelled and crushed a Mamluk cavalry charge led by Janbirdi al-Ghazali, heavily relying on Ottoman firepower to secure the path toward Egypt
casualties: Heavy Mamluk casualties and captures, with only a fraction escaping under al-Ghazali

name: Battle of Brahynivka / related engagements
commanders: Tatar-Cossack coalition vs. Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth
importance: Series of engagements reflecting shifting alliances in Ukraine during the Ruin period.

name: Battle of Ochmatów
commanders: Stanisław Koniecpolski vs. Tuhay Bey / Crimean Tatars
importance: Brilliant winter campaign by Koniecpolski that completely shattered the Tatar invading force using superior artillery and tactical positioning.

name: Oruç Reis seizes Algiers
commanders: Oruç Reis (Barbarossa) vs. Local rulers / Spanish garrison
importance: Established Algiers as the primary base of Ottoman corsair power in the western Mediterranean.

name: Battle of Formentera
commanders: Hayreddin Barbarossa vs. Spanish fleet
importance: Major naval victory for Hayreddin Barbarossa against Rodrigo Portuondo's Spanish fleet.

name: Charles V's conquest of Tunis
commanders: Charles V vs. Hayreddin Barbarossa
importance: Temporary Spanish capture of Tunis and destruction of Barbarossa's fleet base.

name: Charles V's failed Algiers expedition
commanders: Charles V vs. Hassan Pasha (Algiers garrison)
importance: Disastrous storm and fierce defense shattered Charles V's massive fleet and expeditionary army.
casualties: Massive Habsburg fleet and troop losses.

name: Fall of Tripoli
commanders: Turgut Reis and Sinan Pasha vs. Knights Hospitaller
importance: Tripoli captured from the Knights Hospitaller, establishing the Ottoman Eyalet of Tripoli.

name: Ottoman Reconquest and Annexation of Tunisia
commanders: Kılıç Ali Pasha & Ciğalazade Yusuf Sinan Pasha vs. Spanish garrison
importance: Permanently annexed Tunisia to Ottoman lands until French occupation in 1881; final direct confrontation between Castilian forces and the Turks for a long period

name: Ottoman-Algerian Capture of Fez (1576)
commanders: Ottoman-Algerian forces
importance: Prompted Portugal's Sebastian I to intervene in Morocco, leading to the Battle of Alcácer Quibir

name: Battle of Alcácer Quibir
commanders: Abu Abdallah Mohammed II Saadi & Portuguese-Spanish-financed forces vs. Ottoman-Algerian-Moroccan coalition
importance: Last major proxy engagement of the Spanish-Ottoman total war era; King Sebastian I of Portugal was killed
casualties: King Sebastian I of Portugal killed; heavy losses on both sides

name: Armistice, Ottomans and Kingdom of Naples
commanders: Martin de Acuña (mediator) for Ottoman Empire & Kingdom of Naples
importance: First formal step toward broader Spanish-Ottoman peace negotiations

name: Draft Ceasefire Agreement (Spain-Ottoman)
commanders: Giovanni Margliani & Bruti (Spain) & Grand Vizier Sokollu Mehmed Pasha (Ottoman)
importance: Formal framework agreement dividing spheres of influence between Ottoman and Spanish-aligned states

name: Spanish-Ottoman Truce Renewals
commanders: Spain & Ottoman Empire
importance: Extended the effective ceasefire in the Mediterranean over more than a decade

name: Castilian War
commanders: Spain (Jolo-based forces) & New World auxiliaries vs. Sultanate of Brunei (Ottoman-aided)
importance: Ottoman expeditionary force of Turks, Egyptians, Berbers, Swahilis, Somalis, Arabs, Iranians, Malays and Moriscos aided Brunei; Spain occupied Brunei but withdrew due to epidemic disease

name: Capture of Muscat (1581)
commanders: Ottoman forces of Yemen
importance: Prompted a Spanish military expedition against Ottoman Egypt in response, via Red Sea raids

name: Spanish Red Sea Raids and Yemen Expedition
commanders: Spanish forces vs. Ottoman Yemen
importance: Aimed to obstruct the India-Jeddah trade route by occupying a strategic island near Aden

name: Ottoman Raid Capturing Spanish Galleys
commanders: Hasan Pasha (Ottoman Governor of Yemen)
importance: Captured 4 Spanish galleys with goods sent to the Sublime Porte as tribute

name: Ottoman Expedition to Mogadishu
commanders: Mir Ali Beg (Ottoman corsair) vs. Portuguese Swahili Coast
importance: Local population submitted to the Sultan; coastal territories (Barawa, Pate, Pemba, Kilwa) supported the Ottomans; Portuguese withdrew to Malindi
casualties: 60 Portuguese captives taken; a Portuguese ship captured

name: Portuguese Fleet Response (Ruy Gonçalves da Câmara)
commanders: Ruy Gonçalves da Câmara (Portugal, 26 vessels) vs. Mir Ali Beg
importance: Failed to catch the Ottoman corsairs; discouraged further aggressive Portuguese strategy in the theater

name: Fleet of Martim Afonso de Melo — Subjection of Faza and Mombasa
commanders: Martim Afonso de Melo (Portugal, 2 galleons, 3 galleys, 13 light-galleys, 650 soldiers)
importance: Restored Portuguese suzerainty over Faza and Mombasa and reaffirmed alliance with Malindi

name: Battle of Mombasa
commanders: Tomé de Sousa Coutinho (Portugal) & Mateus de Vasconcelos vs. Mir Ali Beg (Ottoman)
importance: Crushed Mir Ali Beg's fort, sacked 3 Turkish galleys with 30 guns, captured Mir Ali Beg, ending the Ottoman project to seize the Portuguese sphere of influence in East Africa
casualties: 3 Ottoman galleys sunk/captured; Mir Ali Beg captured

name: Capture of Mombasa (1631-32)
commanders: Yusuf ibn al-Hasan (Sultanate of Mombasa, minor Ottoman aid) vs. Portuguese
importance: Portuguese briefly expelled from the region of modern Kenya

name: Anti-Ottoman Revolts of 1565-1572
commanders: Spanish-backed Balkan Christian networks vs. Ottoman rule
importance: Part of a wider Spanish intrigue network among Eastern Orthodox Christians to seed future anti-Ottoman revolts

name: Albanian Revolt
commanders: Albanian rebels (Spanish-linked) vs. Ottoman rule
importance: Part of the Spanish-backed network of anti-Ottoman revolts among Balkan Christians

name: Himara Revolt
commanders: Himariote rebels (Spanish-linked) vs. Ottoman rule
importance: Continuation of Spanish-Habsburg intrigue among Albanian Christians against Ottoman rule

name: Thessaly Rebellion
commanders: Greek rebels (Spanish-linked) vs. Ottoman rule
importance: Part of the broader pattern of Spanish-fostered anti-Ottoman Balkan revolts

name: Epirus Revolt
commanders: Epirote rebels (Spanish-linked) vs. Ottoman rule
importance: Continued the pattern of Spanish-fostered revolt among Balkan Orthodox Christians

name: Spanish-Genoese Campaign against Ottoman Tunisia
commanders: Giovanni Andrea Doria (Spain-Genoa) vs. Ottoman Tunisia
importance: Marked the shift of the conflict's focus from the eastern Mediterranean to northwest Africa

name: Campaign against Algiers (1601-1608)
commanders: Spain (with Kingdom of Kuku & Kabylians under Amar ben Amar) vs. Ottoman-Algerian defenders
importance: Extended attempt to conquer Algiers with local Kabylian allies ultimately failed

name: Battle of the Gulf of Cadiz
commanders: Barbary corsairs (with former Elizabethan Sea Dogs) vs. Spanish shipping
importance: Marked renewed Anglo-Barbary piracy against Spain after the end of the Anglo-Spanish War

name: Naval Actions at Longo Island (Kos)
commanders: Spanish forces vs. Ottoman forces
importance: Minor naval action in North Africa/Aegean theater during the shift to corsair warfare

name: Battle of Hammamet
commanders: Spanish forces vs. Ottoman-Tunisian forces
importance: Ended in failure for Spain during the corsair warfare period

name: Raid on Durazzo
commanders: Spanish forces vs. Ottoman Albania
importance: Attempted to disrupt improving Venetian-Ottoman relations by raiding the Albanian coast

name: Twelve Years' Truce
commanders: Spain & Dutch Republic
importance: Diluted the Anglo-Dutch-French-Barbary alliance against Spain; also marked the start of the Franco-Algerian War

name: Franco-Algerian War Begins
commanders: France vs. Ottoman-Algerian corsairs
importance: Sometimes saw Spain and France cooperate militarily in the Mediterranean during this period

name: Raid on La Goulette (Luis Fajardo)
commanders: Luis Fajardo (Spain)
importance: Fajardo also raided Mazalquivir and Tlemcen and transported expelled Moriscos to Oran during this campaign

name: Raiding of Mazalquivir and Tlemcen
commanders: Luis Fajardo (Spain)
importance: Conducted before Fajardo's La Goulette raid, part of the same campaign

name: Capture of Larache
commanders: Marquis of San Germán (Spain), ceded by al-Ma'mun of Morocco
importance: Al-Ma'mun ceded the port to Spain for help in Moroccan dynastic struggle; aimed to preserve Moroccan independence from Ottoman occupation and end the Barbary slave trade axis

name: Raid on Kerkennah
commanders: Alvaro de Bazán (Spain) vs. Ottoman-Tunisian corsair base
importance: Overran the corsair base in the Kerkennah Islands, freeing Christian captives

name: Raid on La Goulette (Antonio Pimentel)
commanders: Antonio Pimentel (Spain, 6 galleys)
importance: Burned seven pirate ships and captured three, destroying newly-built Ottoman-style ships intended for Atlantic raids

name: Battle of Focchies
commanders: Giacomo da Riva vs. Ottoman Fleet Commander
importance: A major naval engagement of the Cretan War in the harbour of Focchies (Foça); a Venetian fleet reinforced by English and Dutch armed merchantmen under Giacomo da Riva decisively breached the Ottoman harbor defenses and destroyed a significant portion of the Ottoman fleet anchored within, though some enemy ships managed to escape and reinforce Crete
casualties: 105 Venetian-allied casualties and two ships lost; devastating losses for the Ottoman fleet including multiple warships, galleasses, and galleys burnt or captured

name: First Battle of the Dardanelles
commanders: Giuseppe Delfino vs. Kara Murat Pasha
importance: The first major naval engagement at the mouth of the Dardanelles during the Cretan War; an Ottoman armada under Kara Murat Pasha overwhelmed and routed a smaller Venetian fleet under Giuseppe Delfino, which had attempted to intercept and blockade the straits
casualties: Venetians lost 2 ships and 1 galley burnt, 1 galley captured, ~30 killed and 40 wounded, with Daniele Morosini captured and Francesco Morosini killed; Ottomans lost 2 sailing ships burnt and several vessels damaged/lost

name: Second Battle of the Dardanelles
commanders: Lazzaro Mocenigo vs. Mustafa Pasha
importance: A clear Venetian victory during the Cretan War; a Venetian fleet under Lazzaro Mocenigo successfully executed a blockade strategy inside the mouth of the Dardanelles Strait, destroying numerous Ottoman sailing ships, galleasses, and galleys while maintaining the blockade against Ottoman resupply
casualties: Venetians lost 1 ship (David Golia) with 126 killed and 180 wounded; Ottomans suffered heavy losses including 11 sailing ships destroyed/wrecked, several galleasses and galleys sunk or burnt, and 358 captured

name: Battle of Cape Corvo
commanders: Ottavio d'Aragona (Spain) vs. Ottoman defenders
importance: Successful raid on the Karaburun Peninsula in modern Turkey

name: Capture of the Zaydani Library
commanders: Spanish Navy vs. French corsair carrying Saadi royal treasures
importance: Intercepted the royal library/treasures of the Saadi dynasty amid Moroccan internal rebellion

name: Capture of La Mámora
commanders: Luis Fajardo (Spain, 20 ships) vs. Dutch corsairs (Muley Zidan-backed pirate haven)
importance: Occupied and renamed the fortress San Miguel de Ultramar; held until Moroccan forces retook it in 1681

name: Battle of Gibraltar
commanders: Jacob van Heemskerk vs. Don Juan de Álvarez de Ávila
importance: Dutch fleet completely destroyed the anchored Spanish fleet in the strait, though distinct from corsair operations, it defined the western Mediterranean naval balance.

name: Turkish Abductions (Grindavík raid)
commanders: Salé/Barbary corsairs vs. Icelandic villagers
importance: Barbary corsairs from Salé raided Grindavík, Iceland, capturing provisions and citizens.

name: Sack of Vestmannaeyjar
commanders: Moroccan/Barbary corsairs vs. Icelandic population
importance: Notorious 'Tyrkjaránið' (Turkish Abductions) where corsairs raided the Westman Islands, taking nearly 400 Icelanders into North African slavery.

name: Sack of Baltimore
commanders: Murat Reis the Younger (Jan Janszoon) vs. English/Irish villagers
importance: Algerine corsairs sacked the coastal village of Baltimore in County Cork, Ireland, carrying almost the entire village population into slavery.

name: Blake's raid on Porto Farina
commanders: Robert Blake vs. Beylicate of Tunis
importance: English fleet sailed into the heavily fortified harbor of Porto Farina (Tunis) and burned the Tripolitan/Tunisian corsair fleet.

name: French bombardment of Algiers
commanders: French Navy vs. Algiers Regency
importance: Early retaliatory French naval bombardment against increasing corsair depredations in the western Mediterranean.

name: Third Battle of the Dardanelles
commanders: Lorenzo Marcello & Gregorio Carafa vs. Kenan Pasha
importance: The heaviest Ottoman naval defeat since Lepanto; an allied Venetian and Maltese fleet under Lorenzo Marcello trapped and annihilated the Ottoman armada inside the Dardanelles, enabling the occupation of Tenedos and Lemnos, tightly blockading the straits, and cutting off supplies to Crete and Constantinople
casualties: Venetian loss of 3 ships and 207 killed, 260 wounded, 94 missing; Malta lost 40 killed and 100+ wounded; Captain General Lorenzo Marcello killed. Catastrophic Ottoman losses of dozens of sailing ships, galleasses, and galleys sunk, burnt, or captured, alongside the liberation of 5,000 Christian slaves.

name: Fourth Battle of the Dardanelles
commanders: Lazzaro Mocenigo vs. Topal Mehmed Pasha
importance: A decisive three-day engagement during the Cretan War where an Ottoman fleet under Topal Mehmed Pasha broke the long-standing Venetian blockade of the Dardanelles, resulting in the death of Venetian commander Lazzaro Mocenigo and allowing the Ottomans to resume resupplying their forces in the Aegean and Crete
casualties: Heavy Venetian losses including the flagship and commander Lazzaro Mocenigo killed by falling debris; significant Ottoman naval losses but successfully achieved their strategic breakthrough

name: French naval bombardment of Algiers
commanders: Abraham Duquesne vs. Algiers defense
importance: First major use of specialized bomb vessels by Duquesne to force Algiers to curb corsair raids against French shipping.

name: French naval bombardment of Algiers (Duquesne)
commanders: Abraham Duquesne vs. Algiers Regency
importance: Continued naval punitive expeditions against Algiers following the breakdown of previous treaties.

name: French naval bombardment of Algiers (Tourville)
commanders: Anne Hilarion de Tourville vs. Algiers Regency
importance: Intense naval bombardment led by Tourville to enforce French terms on the Regency.

name: Hadım Suleiman Pasha's expedition against Diu
commanders: Hadım Suleiman Pasha vs. Portuguese garrison
importance: Major Ottoman naval expedition staging through the Red Sea to challenge Portuguese hegemony in western India.

name: Ottoman capture of Aden
commanders: Ottoman naval forces vs. Local Yemeni rulers
importance: Secured the vital chokepoint at the mouth of the Red Sea, firmly establishing the Eyalet of Yemen.

name: Siege and devastation of Georgian fortresses
commanders: Ottoman regional forces vs. Georgian kingdoms of Kartli-Kakheti
importance: Part of the extensive Ottoman-Safavid frontier campaigns where Ottoman forces besieged, captured, and devastated key border fortresses in the Georgian borderlands.
casualties: Heavy local garrison and regional losses.

name: Siege of Tiflis (Tbilisi)
commanders: Lala Mustafa Pasha vs. Safavid garrison
importance: Successful Ottoman capture and fortification of Tbilisi, securing a vital administrative and military hub in eastern Georgia.

name: Battle near Shirvan and Derbent
commanders: Adil Giray (Crimean Tatars) & Ottoman forces vs. Safavid forces
importance: Joint Ottoman-Crimean campaign securing the northern Caucasus corridor down to Derbent, though Prince Adil Giray was captured later in the campaign.

name: Ottoman coastal raids into Imereti and Guria
commanders: Ottoman Black Sea fleet/regional forces vs. Western Georgian kingdoms
importance: Repeated maritime and amphibious punitive raids along the eastern Black Sea coast enforcing Ottoman hegemony over Imereti, Guria, and Mingrelia.

name: Crimean Tatar Caucasus reinforcement campaigns
commanders: Crimean Khanate contingents vs. Safavid regional forces
importance: Repeated tactical marches by Crimean Tatars through Dagestan and Shirvan to secure the northern flank of Ottoman operations during the 1578–1590 Ottoman-Safavid War.

name: Construction and garrisoning of Kars Fortress
commanders: Ottoman imperial engineers vs. Regional frontier forces
importance: Massive reconstruction and massive garrisoning of Kars as an advanced forward staging base for deeper Caucasian and Iranian campaigns.

name: Battle of Torches
commanders: Özdemiroğlu Osman Pasha vs. Safavid forces
importance: Fought largely at night illuminated by torches in Shirvan; secured total Ottoman control over the eastern Caucasus and Dagestan.

name: Piri Reis's campaign against Muscat and Hormuz
commanders: Piri Reis vs. Portuguese garrison
importance: Piri Reis led the Ottoman fleet out of Red Sea bases to strike at Portuguese strongholds in Muscat and the Persian Gulf approaches.

name: Battle of Cape Gelidonya
commanders: Francisco de Rivera (Spain, 6 galleons, sent by Viceroy Osuna) vs. larger Ottoman fleet
importance: Described as a 'little Lepanto'; Spanish galleons inflicted heavy losses on a much larger Ottoman force off Anatolia
casualties: Heavy Ottoman losses (not quantified in source)

name: Battle of Cape Palos
commanders: Spanish convoy (from Cartagena) vs. Sulayman Reis (16 Algerine galleys)
importance: Spanish troop convoy ambushed and overwhelmed by the Dutch-Algerian admiral
casualties: Spain lost two ships and about 700 men

name: Battle of Ragusa
commanders: Venetian (Giovanni faction, anti-Habsburg) forces vs. Spanish-aligned interests
importance: Part of the Uskok War tensions in the Adriatic, a prelude to the Thirty Years' War

name: Siege of Coron (1533–1534)
commanders: Andrea Doria & Jerónimo Mendoza vs. Lütfi Pasha
result: Imperial Victory (First Siege) / Ottoman Victory & Evacuation (Second Siege)
importance: A major two-part conflict during the Ottoman–Habsburg wars; an imperial relief armada under Andrea Doria brilliantly routed Lütfi Pasha's Ottoman fleet and lifted the first siege of Coron in August 1533, though the garrison was ultimately evacuated and the fortress returned to Ottoman control the following year due to strategic overextension
casualties: 400 Imperial soldiers killed, 300 captured; 1 galley sunk and several ships captured/damaged on the Ottoman side

name: Battle of Gibraltar (Dutch-Barbary Related, 1618)
commanders: Dutch/Barbary-aligned forces vs. Spanish forces
importance: Listed among the Adriatic/Mediterranean engagements tied to Venetian anti-Habsburg maneuvering

name: Dutch-Barbary War (Brief Cooperation Phase)
commanders: Mooy Lambert & Miguel de Vidazábal (Dutch-Spanish cooperation) vs. Corsairs of Algiers
result: Ended when the Eighty Years' War resumed
importance: Rare instance of brief Dutch-Spanish cooperation against Barbary corsairs

name: English Expedition to Algiers
commanders: Kingdom of England vs. Ottoman-Algerian corsairs
importance: Its failure led to renewed Anglo-Turkish piracy against Habsburg Spain

name: Battle of Chios (1621)
commanders: Carlo Doria (Spanish-Italian-Flemish) vs. Ottoman fleet
importance: Triumph in the Aegean Sea early in the reign transition to Philip IV

name: Battle of Gibraltar (1621)
commanders: Fadrique de Toledo (Spain) vs. Dutch-Danish navy
importance: Defeated a Dutch-Danish navy before it could combine forces with the Corsairs of Algiers

name: Relief of Genoa
commanders: Carlo Doria (12 reinforced galleys) vs. France
importance: Spanish galleys stationed at Monaco and Finale Ligure took action defending Genoa against France while also patrolling against Ottoman threats

name: Battle of the Gulf of Tunis
commanders: Marquess of Santa Cruz (Spanish-Maltese fleet) vs. Tunisian corsair fleet
importance: Captured all fourteen enemy galleys off Tunis

name: Battle of Palermo (1624)
commanders: Marquess of Santa Cruz/Bazán (Spain) vs. Barbary armada
importance: Despite being outnumbered, Christians sank seven and captured six corsair ships, freeing 400 galley-slaves
casualties: 7 corsair ships sunk, 6 captured; 400 Christian slaves freed

name: Battle of the Dalmatian Coast
commanders: Spanish-led force (with Genoese and Maltese allies) vs. Algerine-Tunisian fleet
importance: Seized seven galleys near Venetian Dalmatia, a clear blow to Ottoman naval power

name: Battle of San Pietro Island
commanders: Diego Pimentel (Spain, Neapolitan and allied galleys) vs. Six Algerine corsairs
importance: Destroyed the flagship and captured four ships near Sardinia

name: Sack of Málaga
commanders: Moroccan corsairs vs. Spanish coastal town
importance: Example of continued Barbary corsair raiding of Spanish coastal towns even as formal fighting tapered off after 1625

name: Franco-Spanish War
commanders: Spain vs. France
importance: Drew Spanish Mediterranean naval focus away from the Ottoman front after 1635

name: Battle of Breadfield
commanders: Pál Kinizsi, István Báthory, Vuk Branković & Basarab Laiotă cel Bătrân vs. Ali Koca Bey & Basarab cel Tânăr
importance: A combined Hungarian, Serbian, and allied army led by Pál Kinizsi and István Báthory decisively defeated a massive Ottoman-Wallachian raiding force, providing decades of security for Transylvania and southern Hungary
casualties: High Ottoman losses (~thousands killed, including Malkoçoğlu and Isa Bey); ~3,000 Hungarian/allied losses

name: Ottoman-Portuguese Red Sea trade skirmishes
commanders: Ottoman Red Sea maritime patrols vs. Portuguese privateers/traders
importance: Low-intensity skirmishing and convoy protection securing Red Sea spice and coffee trade routes against Portuguese interception.

name: Corsair raid on the Canary Islands
commanders: Barbary corsairs vs. Spanish Atlantic garrisons
importance: Demonstrated the expanding operational reach of North African corsairs into the Atlantic archipelagos.

name: Salé corsair raid on Cornwall
commanders: Salé (Moroccan) rovers vs. English coastal settlements
importance: Salé corsairs raided Mount's Bay and the Cornish coastline, highlighting the vulnerability of English shipping and shores.
casualties: Coastal property damage and captives taken.

name: Turkish Abductions (Grindavík raid)
commanders: Barbary/Salé corsairs vs. Danish-Icelandic villagers
importance: Opening phase of the 'Tyrkjaránið' (Turkish Abductions), where corsairs raided Grindavík and local Icelandic coastal settlements.

name: Sack of Vestmannaeyjar
commanders: Barbary/Salé corsairs vs. Icelandic island population
importance: The most notorious northern Atlantic corsair raid; several hundred inhabitants of the Westman Islands were abducted into North African slavery.

name: Sack of Baltimore
commanders: Murat Reis the Younger (Jan Janszoon) vs. Irish villagers
importance: Algerine corsairs sacked the coastal village of Baltimore in County Cork, Ireland, carrying almost the entire village population into captivity.

name: Corsair raids on British coastal waters
commanders: North African corsairs vs. Irish, Cornish, and Devon coastal guards
importance: Repeated corsair deep-water incursions along the Irish, Cornish, and Devon coastlines, disrupting regional commerce.

name: Salé Rovers raiding in the English Channel
commanders: Salé Rovers vs. English shipping / coastal approaches
importance: Persistent raiding by Moroccan Salé rovers into the English Channel and southwest England approaches.

name: Raid on Trabzon
commanders: Prince Selim vs. Ibrahim (Safavid)
importance: First direct military clash between the Ottomans and Safavids; Prince Selim repelled the raid and pursued them to Erzincan.

name: Selim's Counterattack on Erzincan
commanders: Prince Selim vs. Safavid regional forces
importance: Independent Ottoman counterattack into Erzincan in response to the Safavid invasion of the Dulkadirids.

name: Selim's Counterattack on Bayburt
commanders: Prince Selim vs. Safavid regional forces
importance: Continuation of Prince Selim's 1507 campaign, defeating local Safavid forces in Bayburt.

name: Raid on Antalya
commanders: Şahkulu vs. Şehzade Korkut
importance: Şahkulu raided Antalya with 400–500 men, causing Şehzade Korkut to flee and abandon his treasury.

name: Skirmish at Antalya
commanders: Serasker Hasan Pasha vs. Şahkulu's rebels
importance: Serasker Hasan Pasha secured the treasury to Antalya but was subsequently attacked, defeated, and forced to retreat.

name: Capture of Burdur & Siege of Adana
commanders: Şahkulu vs. Murad Pasha
importance: Rebels captured Isparta and attacked Burdur, killing sanjakbey Murad Pasha alongside 2,000 men; an initial siege of Adana was also launched.

name: Ambush at Kütahya
commanders: Hadım Ali Pasha & Karagöz Ahmet Pasha vs. Şahkulu
importance: Şahkulu ambushed and nearly annihilated an Ottoman army sent by Bayezid II, capturing and executing Karagöz Ahmet Pasha.
casualties: Heavy Ottoman losses, senior commander executed

name: Battle of Manisa & Siege of Kütahya
commanders: Şehzade Korkut & Haydar Pasha vs. Şahkulu
importance: After a brief setback at Kütahya against Haydar Pasha, Şahkulu invaded Manisa, routed Şehzade Korkut, and killed Serasker Hasan Pasha.
casualties: High Ottoman casualties including senior leaders

name: Second Attack on Kütahya
commanders: Haydar Pasha vs. Şahkulu
importance: Şahkulu returned to Kütahya in a follow-up engagement and killed Haydar Pasha.

name: Battle near Ankara
commanders: Kâtip Ali Pasha vs. Şahkulu
importance: Major field battle where an Ottoman army of 50,000 under Kâtip Ali Pasha was defeated by the rebels, and the Ottoman commander was killed.

name: Skirmish in Karaman
commanders: Haydar Pasha & Cündî Kemal Bey vs. Şahkulu
importance: During his retreat toward Safavid territories, Şahkulu attacked Karaman, killing beylerbey Haydar Pasha and sanjakbey Cündî Kemal Bey.
casualties: Severe leadership casualties for the Ottomans

name: Battle at Sivas / Çubukova
commanders: Hadım Ali Pasha vs. Şahkulu
importance: Hadım Ali Pasha pursued Şahkulu for 14 days culminating in a fierce battle where the Ottomans were defeated and Ali Pasha was killed (though Şahkulu was also fatally wounded, breaking the revolt).
casualties: Heavy casualties on both sides; death of Grand Vizier/Commander Hadım Ali Pasha

name: Clash at Eyüyazı
commanders: Nur-Ali Khalifa vs. Hadım Sinan Pasha
importance: Nur-Ali Khalifa defeated an Ottoman army led by vizier Hadım Sinan Pasha, resulting in the death of commander Yularkıstı Sinan Pasha.

name: Attempted Capture of Urfa
commanders: Murad Bey vs. Acheh Soltan Qajar
importance: Sultan Selim's 8,000-man force under Murad Bey failed to capture Urfa and was repelled by the city's governor, with Murad Bey killed.

name: Siege and Capture of Bayburt
commanders: Bıyıklı Mehmed Bey & Mustafa Bey vs. Kara Maksud-i
importance: Joint Ottoman forces successfully besieged and captured Bayburt after the governor refused to surrender.

name: Surrender of Kiğı
commanders: Bıyıklı Mehmed Bey vs. Kiğı Governor
importance: Kiğı Castle surrendered peacefully without a siege after its governor transmitted the keys directly to Bıyıklı Mehmed Bey.

name: Battle of Ovacık
commanders: Pir Hüseyin Bey & Bıyıklı Mehmed Pasha vs. Nur-Ali Khalifa & Aykutoğlu Muhammed Bey
importance: An Ottoman army of 10,000 under Pir Hüseyin Bey and Bıyıklı Mehmed Pasha defeated Nur-Ali Khalifa and Aykutoğlu Muhammed Bey, resulting in the death of Nur-Ali Khalifa and the annexation of Tunceli.
casualties: Heavy Safavid casualties, Nur-Ali Khalifa killed

name: Siege and Capture of Diyarbakır
commanders: Cemşid Bey, Yiğit Ahmet, Şadi Pasha & Idris Bitlisi vs. Karahan Ustajli & Durmuş Bey
importance: An Ottoman army defeated a Safavid force of 10,000 under Karahan Ustajli and Durmuş Bey, successfully capturing the city of Diyarbakır.

name: Siege and Capture of Harput
commanders: Çerkes Hüseyin Bey & Karaçinoğlu Ahmet Bey vs. Safavid Garrison
importance: 1,000 Janissaries successfully captured Harput after a rapid 3-day siege.

name: Ambush at Sinjar
commanders: Pro-Ottoman Kurdish fighters vs. Çuka Khan (Safavid)
importance: 500 pro-Ottoman Kurdish fighters ambushed a 2,000-strong Safavid force under Çuka Khan, inflicting casualties with minimal losses.

name: Ambush at Bismil
commanders: Karahan Ustajli vs. Çerkez Hüseyin Bey & Mehmed Çelebi
importance: Karahan Ustajli ambushed an Ottoman force in revenge, annihilating the entire Ottoman contingent and killing the sanjakbey of Harput, Çerkez Hüseyin Bey, and Mehmed Çelebi.
casualties: Entire Ottoman force wiped out, senior commanders killed

name: Battle of Koçhisar
commanders: Bıyıklı Mehmed Pasha vs. Karahan Ustajli
importance: Bıyıklı Mehmed Pasha led 20,000 Ottomans to a decisive field victory against 6,000 Safavids, resulting in the death of the Safavid commander Karahan Ustajli.

name: Battle of Marj Dabiq
commanders: Sultan Selim I vs. Sultan Al-Ashraf Qansuh al-Ghawri
importance: A decisive clash ending Mamluk supremacy. Following months of diplomatic ruses, Sultan Selim I's artillery-backed forces crushed Qansuh al-Ghawri's army near Aleppo, opening the gate to the conquest of Syria and Egypt.
casualties: Catastrophic Mamluk losses; Sultan Qansuh al-Ghawri perished on the field alongside thousands of cavalrymen.

name: Siege and Capture of Mardin
commanders: Bıyıklı Mehmed Pasha & Deli Husrev Pasha vs. Ustajli Süleyman Bey
importance: Bıyıklı Mehmed Pasha and Deli Husrev Pasha captured Mardin after an extended siege involving heavy artillery; the Safavid commander Ustajli Süleyman Bey was killed.
casualties: Heavy garrison losses, Safavid commander killed

name: Capture of Hasankeyf
commanders: Idris Bitlisi & Bıyıklı Mehmed Pasha vs. Hasankeyf Garrison
importance: Idris Bitlisi and Bıyıklı Mehmed Pasha successfully besieged and captured Hasankeyf, taking its governor and defenders prisoner.

name: Capture of Mosul
commanders: Bıyıklı Mehmed Pasha & Bedir Bey vs. Ahmed Bey Afshar
importance: Bıyıklı Mehmed Pasha and Bedir Bey defeated Ahmed Bey Afshar and captured Mosul, successfully concluding the Mesopotamia Campaign.

name: Siege of Van
commanders: Suleiman the Magnificent, Rüstem Pasha & Gabriel de Luetz d'Aramon vs. Shah Tahmasp I
importance: Occurred during Suleiman's second campaign of the Ottoman-Safavid War (1532–1555). The walled city of Van was besieged and heavily bombarded, with French ambassador Gabriel de Luetz providing critical advice on artillery placement.
casualties: Safavid garrison defeated and city captured

name: Capture of Bitlis
commanders: Grand Vizier Ibrahim Pasha vs. Safavid Garrison
importance: Conducted during the early incursions of the Ottoman-Safavid conflict, where Grand Vizier Ibrahim Pasha successfully attacked Safavid-held regions and recaptured the strategically vital fortified city of Bitlis.

name: Invasion of Persia by Alqas Mirza
commanders: Alqas Mirza vs. Shah Tahmasp I
importance: Alqas Mirza (Tahmasp's defected half-brother) led a 40,000-strong Ottoman-backed cavalry force to invade Persia, while Tahmasp responded with a devastating scorched-earth policy across Armenia.
casualties: Extensive regional devastation and troop losses

name: Battle near the Euphrates
commanders: Ottoman forces vs. Persian forces & Portuguese allies
importance: Portuguese forces intervened to assist the Persians, deploying tactical troops and twenty cannons to help defeat an Ottoman army near the Euphrates.

name: Fort Captures in Georgia and Tabriz Gains
commanders: Suleiman the Magnificent vs. Regional Garrisons
importance: During the continuation of the second campaign, Sultan Suleiman successfully secured various strategic forts in Georgia and captured territorial gains around Tabriz and Persian-ruled Armenia.
casualties: Garrisons captured or forced to surrender

name: Safavid Incursions in Eastern Anatolia
commanders: Safavid forces vs. Ottoman regional garrisons
result: Safavid raid success / Triggered Ottoman retaliation
importance: Safavid attacks devastated Van and Erzurum, resulting in heavy casualties among the local population and triggering Sultan Suleiman's final campaign of the war.

name: Ottoman Raid on Safavid Azerbaijan
commanders: Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent vs. Safavid forces
importance: The Ottoman army pushed deep into Safavid Azerbaijan, destroying imperial infrastructure, palaces, and gardens, and taking thousands of captives.

name: Capture of Yerevan
commanders: Ottoman imperial forces vs. Safavid garrison
importance: Yerevan was captured by Ottoman forces during the 1554 campaign phase of the third Ottoman-Safavid war.

name: Capture of Karabakh
commanders: Ottoman imperial forces vs. Safavid regional defenders
importance: Karabakh was successfully invested and captured by Ottoman forces during their strategic push into the southern Caucasus.

name: Battle of Circassia (1501 Expedition)
commanders: Şehzade Mehmed & Mehmed Giray vs. Circassian Forces
importance: Ottoman-Crimean punitive expedition destroyed; Kefe garrison wiped out and Mehmed Giray forced to flee
casualties: Entire Ottoman force (~500 men) and majority of Tatar/Cossack troops killed

name: Skirmish and Counterattack near Azov
commanders: Circassian Force vs. Auz Cherkas & Karabay
importance: Circassians used a feigned retreat to lure and destroy Azov Cossack pursuers, killing both commanders during a retaliatory raid
casualties: ~30 Azov Cossacks killed including leaders Auz Cherkas and Karabay

name: Ottoman Campaign in Western Circassia (1502)
commanders: Ottoman Empire vs. Western Circassia
importance: Second successive Ottoman expedition into western Circassia that ended in failure and defeat

name: Kabardian Expedition (1504)
commanders: Şehzade Mehmed vs. Kabardia
importance: Third expedition led by Şehzade Mehmed without Crimean support, which collapsed after Mehmed was poisoned on Bayezid II's orders

name: Battle of Khotyn (1509)
commanders: Mikołaj Kamieniecki vs. Copaciu
importance: Polish forces retreating from an unsuccessful siege of Suceava successfully repelled and routed a surprise Moldavian-Ottoman attack while crossing the Dniester near Khotyn
casualties: Heavy Moldavian losses, including fifty dignitaries beheaded during the pursuit

name: Battle of Brașov
commanders: Radu Șerban & György Rácz vs. Mózes Székely
importance: Wallachian and Habsburg forces decisively defeated the Ottoman-backed Transylvanian army of Mózes Székely, who was killed in the battle, allowing Radu Șerban to briefly control Transylvania
casualties: Heavy losses for Székely's army; Mózes Székely killed

name: Siege of Velikiye Luki
commanders: Stephen Báthory vs. Ivan Vasiliyevich
importance: Forces of Stephen Báthory successfully besieged and captured the Russian fortress of Velikiye Luki, cutting links between Livonia and Russia
casualties: Thousands of Russian soldiers and civilians killed; ~200 Polish-Hungarian troops killed by a secondary gunpowder magazine explosion

name: Battle of Suceava (1595)
commanders: Jan Potocki & Ieremia Movilă vs. Ştefan Răzvan
importance: A smaller Polish-Lithuanian force under Jan Potocki decisively defeated the Transylvanian-Ottoman forces of Ştefan Răzvan near Suceava during the Moldavian Magnate Wars, leading to Răzvan's capture and execution
casualties: Heavy Transylvanian losses; Răzvan captured and impaled

name: Siege of Brno (1645)
commanders: Jean-Louis Raduit de Souches & Martin Středa vs. Lennart Torstensson & Sigismund II Rákóczi
importance: A small garrison of ~1,400 defenders successfully withstood a months-long siege by 28,000 Swedish and Transylvanian troops, halting Torstensson's march on Vienna

name: Capture of Warsaw (1657)
commanders: George II Rákóczi, Gustaf Otto Stenbock & Anton Zhdanovych vs. Eliasz Jan Łącki
importance: Allied forces besieged and captured Warsaw following the betrayal of the garrison commander, leading to a temporary occupation and sacking of the city
casualties: Garrison and civilian losses during the capture and sacking

name: Siege of Danzig (1577)
commanders: Stephen Báthory vs. Danzig forces
importance: A six-month siege of Danzig by Stephen Báthory ending in a compromise after the Danzig army was defeated in a field battle, with Báthory confirming the city's special privileges in exchange for reparations and recognition
casualties: Heavy losses for Danzig's mercenary army in field engagements

name: Battle for the Sich at Mykytyn Rih
commanders: Bohdan Khmelnytsky vs. Crown Army/Registered Cossack garrison
importance: Opening action of the uprising; defeat of the royal garrison led Registered Cossacks to defect to Khmelnytsky, who was elected Hetman shortly after
casualties: Not specified in the source text

name: Battle of Zhovti Vody
commanders: Bohdan Khmelnytsky & Tugay Bey vs. Stefan Potocki
importance: First major battle of the uprising; Registered Cossack regiments defected mid-engagement, and the Polish camp was encircled and routed
casualties: Not specified in the source text

name: Battle of Korsun
commanders: Bohdan Khmelnytsky & Maksym Kryvonis & Tugay Bey vs. Mikołaj Potocki & Marcin Kalinowski
importance: Both Crown and Field Hetmans captured; combined with the death of King Władysław IV, left Poland leaderless and opened the way for Khmelnytsky's westward march
casualties: Most Polish soldiers perished during the ambush and retreat

name: Siege of Lviv (first)
commanders: Bohdan Khmelnytsky vs. city defenders of Lviv
importance: Demonstrated the reach of the Cossack army into Galicia; ransom funds were used partly to pay Tatar allies
casualties: Not specified in the source text

name: Battle of Pyliavtsi
commanders: Bohdan Khmelnytsky vs. Władysław Dominik Zasławski, Mikołaj Ostroróg & Aleksander Koniecpolski
importance: Annihilation of the Polish infantry caused a panicked flight of the entire crown army and its commanders; Cossacks captured over 90 cannons and vast supplies
casualties: Polish infantry largely annihilated; Cossacks captured goods valued at 7–10 million złotys

name: Siege of Zamość
commanders: Bohdan Khmelnytsky vs. Zamość garrison
importance: Capture of Zamość would have opened the road to Warsaw; siege ended after King John II Casimir's election and request for a ceasefire
casualties: Not specified in the source text

name: Siege of Bar
commanders: Not specified in the source text
result: Not specified in the source text
importance: Renewed hostilities around Bar in Podolia during the buildup to the 1649 campaign
casualties: Not specified in the source text

name: Siege of Zbarazh
commanders: Bohdan Khmelnytsky vs. Adam Firlej
result: Siege lifted following the Treaty of Zboriv
importance: Polish relief force was ambushed while marching to relieve the besieged fortress, leading directly to the Battle of Zboriv
casualties: Not specified in the source text

name: Battle of Zboriv
commanders: Bohdan Khmelnytsky & Islam III Giray vs. King John II Casimir Vasa
importance: King himself was nearly surrounded; led to the Treaty of Zboriv, granting autonomy to Kyiv, Bratslav and Chernihiv voivodeships
casualties: Crown army lost up to 7,000 men

name: Clash at Syni Vody
commanders: Cossack forces vs. Crimean Tatar raiders
importance: Direct confrontation with nominally allied Tatars who continued raiding the civilian population despite Cossack protests

name: Battle of Berestechko
commanders: Bohdan Khmelnytsky & Islam III Giray vs. King John II Casimir Vasa & Jeremi Wiśniowiecki
importance: One of the largest battles of 17th-century Europe; flight of the Tatars and capture of Khmelnytsky's treasury and regalia turned the tide against the Cossacks, though the army recovered within two months
casualties: Over 8,000 Cossack soldiers perished; Poles captured most of the Cossack artillery and gunpowder

name: Confrontation at Bila Tserkva
commanders: Bohdan Khmelnytsky vs. Commonwealth forces
importance: Both sides exhausted after Berestechko; resulting treaty limited the Cossack registry to 20,000 and restricted autonomy to Kyiv Voivodeship, though it was never ratified
casualties: Not specified in the source text

name: Battle of Batih
commanders: Bohdan Khmelnytsky (Tatar cavalry) vs. Marcin Kalinowski
importance: Revenge for Berestechko; Kalinowski killed and half his hussars destroyed; followed by the mass execution of Polish prisoners known as the Batih massacre
casualties: Marcin Kalinowski and half of his hussars killed; Polish prisoners of war massacred afterward

name: Siege of Suceava
commanders: Tymish (Tymofiy) Khmelnytsky vs. Gheorghe Stefan, Transylvanian & Wallachian forces
importance: Tymish Khmelnytsky died in the siege while defending his father-in-law Vasile Lupu's claim to the Moldavian throne, ending Bohdan Khmelnytsky's dynastic ambitions in Moldova

name: Siege of Zhvanets
commanders: Bohdan Khmelnytsky & Islam III Giray vs. King John II Casimir Vasa
importance: Roughly equal-sized armies (~40,000 each) blockaded each other until the Crimean khan brokered a new peace treaty signed 17 December 1653
casualties: Not specified in the source text

name: Cossack-Muscovite campaign in Belarus
commanders: Ivan Zolotarenko (with Muscovite forces) vs. Commonwealth garrisons
importance: 18,000-strong Cossack force occupied Bykhaw, Krychaw and Mogilev in 1654, then advanced to Svislach and Minsk in 1655, later joining Muscovite forces toward Vilnius and Grodno
casualties: Not specified in the source text

name: Polish-Tatar raid into Bratslav and Uman
commanders: Seweryn Potocki (with allied Tatar forces) vs. local Cossack/civilian population
importance: Devastated Podolia and delayed Khmelnytsky's planned offensive into Volhynia; forced thousands of refugees to flee to Moldova
casualties: Not specified in the source text

name: Battle of Okhmativ
commanders: Bohdan Khmelnytsky & Vasily Sheremetev vs. Crown army
importance: Fought amid severe frost; succeeded in halting the Polish advance despite no decisive winner
casualties: Not specified in the source text

name: Siege of Lviv (second)
commanders: Bohdan Khmelnytsky & Vasily Buturlin vs. city defenders of Lviv
importance: A Tatar raid into Khmelnytsky's rear forced the lifting of the siege in exchange for a payment rather than capture of the city
casualties: Not specified in the source text

name: Blockade of Kerch
commanders: Cossack forces vs. Crimean Tatar forces
importance: Prevented 100,000 Tatars from carrying out a large-scale raid into Ukraine and led to devastation of Crimean settlements in retaliation for continued Tatar raiding
casualties: Not specified in the source text

name: Battle of Cornul lui Sas
commanders: Ștefan IX Tomșa & Khan Temir vs. Stefan Potocki & Constantin Movilă
importance: Decisive defeat of Stefan Potocki's private Polish-backed army during the Moldavian Magnate Wars, securing Ștefan Tomșa's rule
casualties: Heavy losses; Stefan Potocki and Elisabeta Movilă captured, Constantin Movilă drowned

name: Crimean Campaign against Kabardia
commanders: Bahadır Giray vs. Kabardian Principality
importance: Catastrophic defeat of the Crimean army under Bahadır Giray after bypassing Taman to strike Kabardia, losing two-thirds of their forces and pausing Crimean offensives
casualties: Approx. two-thirds of the Crimean army lost (~20,000 troops); minor Circassian losses

name: Battle of Udycz
commanders: Stanisław Żółkiewski vs. Khan Temir
importance: Hetman Stanisław Żółkiewski decisively defeated Khan Temir's invading Tatar horde near the Udych River
casualties: Heavy losses for Khan Temir's forces

name: Battle of Sudbischi
commanders: Devlet I Giray vs. Ivan Sheremetyev & Alexey Basmanov
importance: A heavily outnumbered Russian force under Ivan Sheremetyev and Alexey Basmanov successfully repelled multiple assaults from Devlet I Giray's massive Crimean-Ottoman army from a fortified wagon laager
casualties: Heavy Russian losses (~1,100 elite boyar children); extremely high Crimean-Ottoman losses

name: Raid and Battle of Gezlev
commanders: Zakhar Kulaga vs. Feti-Giray
importance: Zaporozhian Cossacks successfully sacked Gezlev (Yevpatoria), but were caught by Feti-Giray's fleet the next morning, resulting in Kulaga's death and capture of several Cossacks
casualties: ~30 Cossacks captured, including the death of ataman Zakhar Kulaga

name: Battle on the Dniester (1589)
commanders: Zaporozhian Cossacks vs. Ğazı Giray
importance: Cossacks intercepted returning Tatar forces from a Galician raiding expedition on the Dniester river
casualties: Heavy losses; ~9,000 Tatar raiders lost and Ğazı Giray wounded, alongside heavy Cossack casualties

name: Battle of Karasubazar (1624)
commanders: Mehmed III Giray & Mykhailo Doroshenko vs. Topal Recep Pasha
importance: Ottoman invasion force landing at Kaffa was ambushed and defeated near Karasubazar by the combined Crimean-Cossack army, halting the attempt to depose Mehmed III Giray
casualties: Heavy Ottoman losses; Hasan Pasha and Ibrahim Pasha killed

name: Battle of Kaffa
commanders: Petro Sahaidachny vs. Ottoman Empire Garrison
importance: A daring naval raid and surprise attack by Zaporizhian Cossacks under Petro Sahaidachny on the heavily fortified Crimean port city of Kaffa; the Cossacks defeated an Ottoman galley squadron, breached the citadel, and liberated thousands of Christian slaves
casualties: Heavy Ottoman garrison casualties and losses of captured ships

name: Battle of Tashiskari
commanders: Giorgi Saakadze & Zaza Tsitsishvili vs. Ottoman and Crimean Tatar forces
importance: Fought near Tashiskari; a Georgian force led by Giorgi Saakadze launched a surprise dawn attack and almost completely destroyed an invading Ottoman and Crimean Tatar army that had raided Kartli to capture King Luarsab II
casualties: Heavy Ottoman and Tatar losses; almost the entire invading force destroyed except for a small number who escaped

name: Battle of Köbölkút
commanders: Ádám Forgách vs. Fazıl Ahmed Pasha
importance: Fought near Köbölkút (modern Gbelce, Slovakia) during the Austro-Turkish War; an Ottoman army under Grand Vizier Fazıl Ahmed Pasha heavily defeated a Habsburg-Hungarian force under Ádám Forgách, enabling the Ottomans to capture the town and extensive territories in modern-day Slovakia
casualties: Heavy Habsburg/Hungarian losses (6,000 killed, 1,000 captured out of 8,000)

name: Battle at Jurjeve Stijene
commanders: Petar Zrinski vs. Ali-Pasha Čengić
importance: Fought in a canyon near Otočac during the Austro-Turkish War; Croatian forces under Petar Zrinski ambushed a larger Ottoman army under Ali-Pasha Čengić, inflicting heavy losses, capturing the Ottoman commander, and halting Ottoman advances into Gacka
casualties: 1,500–2,000 Ottoman killed and hundreds captured, including Ali-Pasha Čengić as a prisoner of war

name: First Battle of Novi Zrin
commanders: Miklós Zrínyi / Nikola Zrinski vs. Kanije Pasha
importance: Fought near the Novi Zrin fortress on the Mura river during the Austro-Turkish War; Croatian and Hungarian forces under Nikola Zrinski sortied from the fortress to rout Kanije Pasha's besieging army, subsequently pursuing and looting the enemy countryside

name: Battle of Vízvár
commanders: Miklós Zrínyi vs. Unknown Ottoman commander
importance: Fought at Vízvár in Csallóköz during the Austro-Turkish War; a 15,000-strong united Christian army including German regiments and led by Miklós Zrínyi ambushed and defeated the Turkish rearguard, capturing equipment, weapons, and livestock
casualties: 600 Turks killed, 20 POWs captured; Christian forces suffered only 12 casualties

name: Battle of Körmend
commanders: Franz III. Nádasdy, Jean de Coligny-Saligny & Wolfgang von Hohenlohe vs. Grand Vizier Ahmed Köprülü
importance: Fought along the Rába River during the Austro-Turkish War; a multinational Christian force successfully held the river fords against Grand Vizier Ahmed Köprülü's army, preventing an Ottoman crossing toward Vienna and setting the stage for the Christian victory at Saint Gotthard
casualties: Heavy Ottoman assault losses; French commander de Coligny wounded

name: Siege of Léva
commanders: Jean-Louis Raduit de Souches vs. Ali Pasha
importance: Fought near Léva (Levice, Slovakia) during the Austro-Turkish War; an Imperial army under Jean-Louis Raduit de Souches ambushed and routed an Ottoman relief force under Ali Pasha, resulting in the death of the Ottoman commander and the capture of artillery and weaponry
casualties: Heavy Ottoman losses, including the death of commander Ali Pasha and abandonment of artillery and carts; light Habsburg casualties

name: Battle of Zsarnóca
commanders: Jean-Louis Raduit de Souches vs. Kücsük Mehmed Pasha
importance: Fought near Zsarnóca (Žarnovica, Slovakia) during the Austro-Turkish War; an Austrian force under Jean-Louis Raduit de Souches repelled and routed an Ottoman division led by Kücsük Mehmed Pasha, resulting in the death of the Ottoman commander and enabling a Habsburg offensive
casualties: Heavy Ottoman losses, including the death of commander Kücsük Mehmed Pasha

name: Siege of Nitra
commanders: Jean-Louis Raduit de Souches & István Koháry vs. Ghazi Hussein & Kurd Mehmed Pasha
importance: Conducted during the Austro-Turkish War; an army under Jean-Louis Raduit de Souches besieged and recaptured the strategic fortress of Nitra from Ottoman forces after intensive artillery bombardment and a negotiated surrender
casualties: Garrison losses during sorties and bombardment; remaining Ottoman defenders granted free retreat

name: Siege of Kanizsa
commanders: Miklós Zrínyi, Wolfgang Julius von Hohenlohe & Pietro Strozzi vs. Sohrab Mehmed Pasha
importance: An unsuccessful month-long siege of the Ottoman fortress of Kanizsa by a combined Christian army led by Miklós Zrínyi; the siege was abandoned due to supply shortages, logistical delays, and the approach of the Grand Vizier's relief army, leading to a hurried Christian retreat
casualties: Unspecified losses during skirmishes and sallies; garrison successfully defended the fortress

name: Destruction of the Suleiman Bridge
commanders: Nikola VII Zrinski (Miklós Zrínyi) & Pál Esterházy vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: A major highlight of Miklós Zrínyi's Winter Campaign during the Austro-Turkish War; Christian cavalry penetrated deep into Ottoman territory and successfully burned the vital 8-kilometer wooden bridge across the Drava River at Osijek, cutting Turkish supply lines
casualties: Minimal Christian losses; minor shelling casualties

name: Capture of Babócsa
commanders: Nikola VII Zrinski & Wolfgang Julius von Hohenlohe vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Fought shortly after the fall of Berzence during Miklós Zrínyi's Winter Campaign; Christian forces successfully captured the strategic Ottoman-held stronghold of Babócsa, clearing the path for the rapid cavalry advance toward Szigetvár and Osijek

name: Capture of Berzence
commanders: Nikola VII Zrinski & Wolfgang Julius von Hohenlohe vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: The initial objective of Miklós Zrínyi's Winter Campaign; allied Christian forces captured the border fortress of Berzence in southwestern Hungary to establish a secure forward base of operations for the deeper push toward the Drava River

name: Siege of Pécs
commanders: Miklós Zrínyi & Wolfgang Julius von Hohenlohe vs. Kaplan Pasha
importance: Fought during Miklós Zrínyi's Winter Campaign; Christian forces successfully sacked the lower city of Pécs but failed to capture the heavily defended citadel due to lack of heavy artillery and poor discipline, ultimately lifting the siege to destroy the Osijek bridge
casualties: Garrison losses during initial assault; heavy Christian losses during disorganized citadel assaults

name: Capture of Nádas
commanders: Independent Christian infantry detachments vs. Ottoman local garrison
importance: Captured during the secondary operations of the 1664 Winter Campaign as Christian forces systematically cleared minor Ottoman-held fortified points in the Danube-Drava confluence

name: Capture of Újvár
commanders: Independent Christian infantry detachments vs. Ottoman local garrison
importance: Secured as part of the wider Danubian offensive by detached Christian units during Miklós Zrínyi's 1664 Winter Campaign, helping clear Ottoman outposts from the area

name: Capture of Szekcső
commanders: Independent Christian infantry detachments vs. Ottoman local garrison
importance: Fought during the Winter Campaign of 1664; Christian troops captured the fortified settlement of Szekcső along the Danube to consolidate control over the region following the raid on the Osijek bridge

name: Capture of Szécs
commanders: Independent Christian infantry detachments vs. Ottoman local garrison
importance: Part of the Danube-Drava estuary operations during Miklós Zrínyi's Winter Campaign; Christian forces occupied the stronghold of Szécs to neutralize local Ottoman resistance and sever regional communications

name: Danube-Drava Estuary Expedition
commanders: Independent Christian infantry units vs. Ottoman local garrisons
importance: Executed concurrently with the Osijek bridge raid during Miklós Zrínyi's Winter Campaign; detached Christian infantry units pushed into the Danube-Drava confluence, successfully occupying and neutralizing the minor Ottoman fortresses of Mohács, Szécs, Szekcső, Újvár, and Nádas to secure the flanks
casualties: Minimal Christian losses; multiple minor Ottoman outposts captured or destroyed

name: Battle of Krasnobród
commanders: Jan Sobieski & Mykhailo Khanenko vs. Selim I Giray
importance: Fought during Jan Sobieski's autumn expedition in the Polish-Ottoman War; Polish and pro-Polish Cossack forces surprised a Tatar camp near Krasnobród after a grueling nocturnal march in heavy rain, destroying several Tatar units and freeing thousands of captive Polish civilians
casualties: Multiple Tatar units destroyed; civilian captives liberated

name: Battle of Niemirów
commanders: Jan III Sobieski vs. Jambet Giray (Azamet Gerej)
importance: Fought during Jan Sobieski's autumn expedition in the Polish-Ottoman War; Crown Hetman Sobieski launched a surprise front-and-rear attack on a large Crimean Tatar camp near Nemyriv, routing the invaders and liberating thousands of captured Polish nobility, peasants, women, and children
casualties: 100 Polish-Lithuanian casualties; 234 Tatars killed and 6,000 captured

name: Battle of Ladyzhyn
commanders: Mykhailo Khanenko & Karol Łużecki vs. Petro Doroshenko & Safa Giray
importance: Fought near Ladyzhyn during the Polish-Ottoman War (1672–76); a combined force of pro-Polish Cossacks and Polish-Lithuanian cavalry under Khanenko and Łużecki defeated an allied force of Crimean Tatars and pro-Doroshenko Cossacks
casualties: Heavy Polish losses during enemy counterattack, alongside opposing Tatar and Cossack casualties

name: Djidjelli Expedition
commanders: François de Vendôme (Duke of Beaufort), Count of Gadagne & Charles-Félix de Galéan vs. Kabyles & Regency of Algiers
importance: A military expedition launched by Louis XIV to seize Djidjelli as a naval base against Barbary corsairs; French forces easily captured the town initially, but internal command disputes, fierce local resistance, supply strains, and an outbreak of plague forced a complete abandonment and demolition of fortifications, followed by the tragic sinking of the returning ship La Lune
casualties: Heavy French losses through ambushes, plague, and over 700 drowned in the shipwreck of La Lune; substantial Kabyle and Algerian losses

name: Capture of Mohács
commanders: Independent Christian infantry detachments vs. Ottoman local garrison
importance: Executed during Miklós Zrínyi's Winter Campaign as detached Christian infantry units swept through the Danube-Drava region, capturing the strategically significant town and fortress of Mohács to secure the army's flank

name: Second Battle of Novi Zrin
commanders: Miklós Zrínyi & Péter Zrínyi vs. Ali Pasha
importance: Fought near the Novi Zrin fortress on the Mura river during the Austro-Turkish War; Hungarian and Croatian forces under Miklós and Péter Zrínyi decisively defeated a 16,000-strong Ottoman army, resulting in the death of Ottoman commander Ali Pasha
casualties: Heavy Ottoman casualties, including the death of commander Ali Pasha

name: Battle of Babadağ (1625)
commanders: Shahin Giray vs. Khan Temir
importance: Shahin Giray was defeated by Khan Temir's Budjak Horde following the collapse of the short-lived Zaporozhian-Crimean alliance
casualties: Heavy losses for Shahin Giray's forces

name: Battle of Kagal'nik (1646)
commanders: Semeon Romanovich Pozharskii vs. Nuraddin (Crimean Khanate)
importance: Russian force led by Pozharskii was defeated near Kagal'nik by a 10,000-strong Crimean army during the failed 1646 campaign
casualties: Heavy Russian losses and subsequent mass desertions due to hunger and demoralization

name: 1480 Sarai Raid
commanders: Vasili Nozdorovaty-Zvenigorodsky & Nur Devlet vs. Great Horde
importance: Joint Russo-Crimean raid on New Sarai while Akhmat Khan was engaged at the Ugra River, forcing his retreat and securing massive loot
casualties: Near-total destruction and capture of the Great Horde capital population/loot

name: Battle and Siege of Kalnyk
commanders: Jan III Sobieski & Mykhailo Khanenko vs. Petro Doroshenko & Tatar allies
result: Tactical Polish Victory / Strategic Cossack-Tatar Defense
importance: Crown Hetman Jan Sobieski defeated a relief force near Kalnyk but ultimately failed to capture the fortified town after a two-week siege
casualties: ~500 Tatar/Cossack troops killed in the relief clash; unknown siege losses

name: Battle of Pidhaitsi (1667)
commanders: John III Sobieski vs. Petro Doroshenko & Crimean Tatars
importance: Hetman John III Sobieski successfully defended against a massive combined Cossack-Tatar force, backed by Ivan Sirko's diversionary expedition into Crimea, leading to an armistice
casualties: Heavy casualties for the invading Tatar-Cossack forces

name: Ottoman-Crimean Invasion of Circassia (1479 Campaign)
commanders: Mengli I Giray & Cezeri Kasim Pasha vs. Peterzeqo & Tabuldu
importance: Crimean Tatars and Ottoman forces captured the strategic coastal fortresses of Anapa and Kopa, establishing early Ottoman influence in the North Caucasus
casualties: Numerous Circassians captured and enslaved; local forces scattered

name: Crimean Campaign against Circassia (1490–1491)
commanders: Mengli I Giray vs. Circassian Tribes
importance: Major campaign by Mengli I Giray launching a systematic series of subdual efforts against the Circassians and Kabardians
casualties: Significant enslavement and devastation in local territories

name: Campaign on Perekop
commanders: Ivan Sirko vs. Karach Bey
importance: Ivan Sirko's 180-strong unit decisively ambushed and destroyed a 1,000-strong Crimean Tatar army, killing Karach Bey and nearly all his men
casualties: Near-total destruction of the Tatar force; negligible Cossack losses

name: Siege of Ochakov (1670)
commanders: Ivan Sirko vs. Ottoman Empire
importance: Ivan Sirko successfully besieged and sacked Ochakov to undermine Ottoman control and demonstrate loyalty to Russia

name: Battle of Sich (1674)
commanders: Ivan Sirko vs. Mehmed IV & Selim I Giray
importance: Cossacks detected and repelled a surprise night assault by an Ottoman-Crimean army of 15,000 Janissaries and 40,000 Tatars sent to destroy the Sich

name: Stand on the Sich (1679)
commanders: Ivan Sirko vs. Ottoman Empire & Crimean Khanate
importance: Joint Cossack-Russian defensive preparations successfully deterred and forced a 25,000-strong Ottoman-Tatar army to retreat from the Sich

name: Siege of Azov (1569)
commanders: Ottoman Fleet vs. Russian/Cossack Defenses
importance: Ottoman fleet besieging Azov was completely destroyed by a violent storm during the 1569 campaign
casualties: Entire Ottoman fleet lost to the storm

name: Pyatigorsk War / Expedition of the Great Horde
